title: ₹1 Crore Opening, ₹65 Crore and Climbing: The Most Beautiful Box Office Surprise of 2026 Belongs to Imtiaz Ali
excerpt: 'Main Vaapas Aaunga' opened to near-empty theatres — sixteen days later, Bengaluru is running at 70% occupancy, the budget is nearly recovered, and Bollywood has its purest word-of-mouth hit in years
body:
Here's a number that should make you uncomfortable: ₹1.15 crore. That's what Main Vaapas Aaunga collected on its opening day. For an Imtiaz Ali film with A.R. Rahman on the soundtrack, Diljit Dosanjh and Naseeruddin Shah leading the cast, and a Partition love story that took years to shape — ₹1.15 crore is not a soft opening. It's a whisper. The kind of number that makes studios quietly start drafting failure press notes.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=PRUTWluKRW8

Sixteen days later, that whisper has become a roar.

As of Day 16, Main Vaapas Aaunga has collected ₹41.80 crore net in India and crossed ₹64.73 crore worldwide, recovering nearly 60% of its ₹70 crore budget. On its third Saturday — competing directly with the opening weekend of Akshay Kumar's Welcome To The Jungle — the film pulled in ₹4.25 crore, a staggering 54% jump from Friday. That figure almost exactly matches Cocktail 2's second Saturday collection. A film that opened at ₹1.15 crore is now matching a Shahid Kapoor starrer that opened at ₹13.50 crore. Head to head. Weekend to weekend.

This doesn't happen in Bollywood anymore. Not like this.

The numbers tell a story of pure, unfiltered audience love — the kind no marketing campaign can manufacture. Week 1 collected ₹12.25 crore. Week 2 nearly doubled it at ₹22.55 crore. That trajectory — growing in the second week instead of collapsing — belongs to a different era of cinema, when films like Rang De Basanti and 3 Idiots built audiences one tearful conversation at a time. Main Vaapas Aaunga is doing exactly that: one Instagram story, one emotional theatre exit, one "you have to watch this" text at a time.

Look at the occupancy numbers and you'll see something extraordinary. On Day 16 — a Saturday in the shadow of a brand-new Akshay Kumar release — Bengaluru was running at 69.5% occupancy, with evening and night shows hitting 82–88%. Hyderabad was at 60%. Chandigarh at 59%. Chennai at 51%. These aren't opening weekend numbers for a blockbuster. These are third-week numbers for a film that had near-empty halls on Day 1. The audience didn't find this film. The film found them — through whispered recommendations and tear-streaked reviews.

"Some stories don't end when the credits roll." — Sharvari, after visiting a theatre with Vedang Raina on Day 16

The film itself is vintage Imtiaz Ali but with a new emotional register — tender where he usually burns hot, patient where he usually aches. Vedang Raina and Sharvari play Keenu and Jiya, young lovers torn apart by 1947, while Diljit Dosanjh and Naseeruddin Shah carry the older timeline with the quiet weight of men who've spent decades remembering a single face. Banita Sandhu, Rajat Kapoor, and Sanjay Suri fill out the ensemble. Rahman's score has been called his most tender in years; the song Kya Kamaal Hai — which arrived from Rahman and lyricist Irshad Kamil almost unbidden during production — has crossed into cultural consciousness the way only a few soundtracks do each decade.

For the diaspora, this film hits different. It's a story about home — about the tree you planted that someone else waters now, the doll left in a trunk, the lane you walked once in Lahore or Sialkot and never again. The overseas gross has already crossed ₹14.90 crore, and the film continues to find screens across the US, UK, and Canada, drawing crowds who see their own grandparents' stories reflected on screen. "Can love really be lost?" the trailer asked. "Can home be taken away from someone's heart?" Sixteen days in, the answer from theatres worldwide is unmistakable.

The next milestone is ₹50 crore net domestically, which should arrive within days. After that, the target becomes The Kerala Story 2's lifetime of ₹52.25 crore. By the time its run ends, Main Vaapas Aaunga could comfortably sit among the top 7 or 8 Bollywood earners of 2026 — a position absolutely nobody would have predicted on June 12.

Imtiaz Ali has always been a filmmaker who believes in feelings over formulas. This time, the audience believed too. They just needed a few days to find the film — and once they did, they wouldn't let it go.
